Mild–moderate has cardiogenic shock; severe has a normal EF
Mild–moderate has rest dyspnea; severe is always asymptomatic
Mild–moderate has no symptoms ± palpitations; severe is symptomatic because of LV failure

questions.sec: Acute versus Chronic AR, Leaflet and Root Causes, the Mild-to-Severe Classification and Compensated Circulatory Changes

questions.q: The mild–moderate chain begins with an incompetent leaflet and incomplete valve closure, then blood leaks from the aorta to the LV and is compensated by ______ with dilatation.
questions.exp: The flow reads incompetent leaflet → incomplete valve closure → blood leaks aorta to LV → compensates with eccentric hypertrophy and dilatation. (Book p313)

questions.sec: Acute versus Chronic AR, Leaflet and Root Causes, the Mild-to-Severe Classification and Compensated Circulatory Changes
questions.q: Which formula and LVEDP status are printed for compensated mild–moderate AR?
opts: EF = ESV/(EDV + ESV), with EF low and LVEDP raised
EF = EDV/ESV, with EF fixed and LVEDP zero
EF = SBP − DBP, with EF low and LVEDP normal
EF = (EDV − ESV)/EDV, with EF normal or increased and LVEDP normal
questions.exp: The printed equation is EF = (end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume)/EDV; EF is N/↑ and LVEDP is N. (Book p313)

questions.sec: Acute versus Chronic AR, Leaflet and Root Causes, the Mild-to-Severe Classification and Compensated Circulatory Changes
questions.q: A patient with chronic mild AR is symptom-free apart from palpitations, and the LV has dilated eccentrically while EF is preserved. Which phase does page 313 describe?
questions.exp: Asymptomatic disease ± palpitations with eccentric hypertrophy/dilatation and normal-to-increased EF is the compensated mild–moderate branch. (Book p313)

questions.sec: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions
questions.q: What happens in the severe or decompensated AR branch?
opts: LV failure gives normal-to-low EF, markedly raised ESV with S3, and markedly raised LVED leading to raised LAP and dyspnea
EF rises indefinitely while pulse pressure narrows
LV failure gives a high EF, low ESV and no dyspnea
The aorta adapts by closing completely and LAP falls
questions.exp: The branch reads LVF → EF (N)/↓, ESV ↑↑↑ (S3+), LVED ↑↑↑ → ↑LAP → dyspnea. (Book p314)

questions.sec: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions

questions.exp: The net-effect column prints preload ↑↑↑, afterload ↑↑, DBP ↓↓↓ and pulse pressure wide. (Book p314)

questions.sec: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions

Afterload follows systolic BP with more blood, more stretch and increased contractility by the Frank–Starling law; pulse pressure is SBP − DBP
Afterload follows LVEDP and pulse pressure is EDV − ESV
Afterload follows coronary flow and pulse pressure is SBP + DBP
questions.exp: The table's dependent-factor cells read α systolic BP: ↑ blood → ↑ stretching → ↑ contractility (Frank–Starling law), and PP = SBP − DBP. (Book p314)

questions.sec: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions

Mayne sign: >15 mmHg; Lincoln sign: liver pulsations

questions.sec: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions
questions.q: Match each symptom to the AS-versus-AR table — 1) Angina 2) Syncope 3) Dyspnea 4) Palpitations … A) AR: + from volume overload; AS: − from pressure overload B) AS: +++ first symptom; AR: + nocturnal only C) AS: +; AR: − D) AS: ++ with raised LVEDP; AR: + with LV failure and raised LVEDP

units.title: Acute versus Chronic AR, Leaflet and Root Causes, the Mild-to-Severe Classification and Compensated Circulatory Changes
units.sec: Acute versus Chronic AR, Leaflet and Root Causes, the Mild-to-Severe Classification and Compensated Circulatory Changes
units.guide:
AR is first divided into acute and chronic disease (p313). Chronic leaflet causes are rheumatic (MS + AR or AR + AS), congenital quadricuspid valves, Takayasu arteritis and ankylosing spondylitis; root causes are syphilis (m/c), Marfan and Ehlers–Danlos syndromes, with rheumatological Takayasu, Behcet, Cogan (aortitis + interstitial keratitis + vestibulitis) and IgG4-related large-vessel vasculitis.
Mild–moderate AR is symptom-free ± palpitations, while severe disease is symptomatic from LV failure. The diastolic gradient is drawn between LV 10 mmHg and aorta 80 mmHg.
An incompetent leaflet fails to close, blood leaks from aorta to LV, and eccentric hypertrophy with dilatation compensates; EF = (EDV − ESV)/EDV remains normal/increased and LVEDP is normal.

units.title: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions
units.sec: Decompensated AR, Circulatory Parameters, Wide Pulse Pressure, Nocturnal Angina, the AS-versus-AR Table and the Pulse Definitions
units.guide:
Decompensated AR moves from LVF to normal/low EF, markedly raised ESV with S3 and markedly raised LVED → raised LAP → dyspnea (p314). Preload rises with blood from LA/LV and aorta/LV, afterload rises with systolic BP/stretch/Frank–Starling contractility, DBP falls as blood regurgitates (it may touch zero) and pulse pressure is wide.
Wide PP produces Hill's >20 mmHg leg–arm difference (surest sign) and Lincoln's prominent popliteal pulsations. Nocturnal angina follows sleeping bradycardia → prolonged diastole → worse coronary steal, while vasoconstriction raises aortic pressure and gradient; hence strict BP control, and exercise tachycardia shortens diastole.
The comparison table gives AS angina +++ first/nocturnal AR +, AS syncope +/AR −, AS dyspnea ++/AR + with LVF and AS palpitations −/AR +. High-volume pulse is increased LV blood → increased EF → increased volume; water-hammer/collapsing pulse is that pulse with routes for exit.

units.title: Collapsing versus Pseudocollapsing Pulses, the Bisferiens Wave, BP and Apex, the Heart-Sound Table and the Early Diastolic Murmur
units.sec: Collapsing versus Pseudocollapsing Pulses, the Bisferiens Wave, BP and Apex, the Heart-Sound Table and the Early Diastolic Murmur
units.guide:
Collapsing pulses are also placed in regurgitation, aorta–pulmonary window and PDA (p315). Collapsing AR has a sharp upstroke/downstroke with ill-sustained apex and high volume; pseudocollapsing MR has normal volume.
Bisferiens has P (percussion) and T (tidal) systolic peaks: P > T means HCM, while P < T or P = T means severe AR ± mild–moderate AS. BP is wide (Hill measured at mid-thigh prone), the apex is hyperdynamic down-and-out and the precordium rocks.
The heart-sound table gives soft S1 from premature closure, root disease loud A2 ± reverse split (P2–A2), valve disease soft A2, S3 only in failure and no S4. The high-pitched soft blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur is at the neo-aortic/3rd left ICS, radiates to axilla (Cole–Cecil), is best heard with the diaphragm at end-expiration while sitting/leaning forward, and leaflet radiation is Key–Hodgkin murmur.

units.title: The Decrescendo Tracing, Ejection Systolic and Austin Flint Murmurs, and the Sixteen Peripheral Signs
units.sec: The Decrescendo Tracing, Ejection Systolic and Austin Flint Murmurs, and the Sixteen Peripheral Signs
units.guide:
The p316 tracing is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur after S2. Associated murmurs are an ESM at the base and a low-pitched mid-diastolic Austin Flint murmur from anterior mitral leaflet displacement by the regurgitant jet.
The 16 peripheral signs, in printed order, are Corrigan (carotid/supraclavicular pulsations), Alfred de Musset (head nodding), Landolfi (pupil-size change), Müller (uvula), Becker (retinal artery), Rosenbach (liver), Gerhardt (spleen), Quincke (digital capillaries), Lighthouse (forehead blanching/flushing), Traube ('pistol shot' femoral sound), Duroziez (to-and-fro femoral murmur with light bell compression), Hill (>20 mmHg leg–arm systolic difference), water-hammer (abruptly collapsing high-volume pulse), Mayne (>15 mmHg DBP fall with arm raised), Lincoln (pulsatile popliteal) and Sherman (unexpected dorsalis pedis prominence after age 75 years).

units.title: Chronic AR Replacement Rules and Acute AR Causes, the No-Time-to-Adapt Pathology, Features and Immediate Treatment
units.sec: Chronic AR Replacement Rules and Acute AR Causes, the No-Time-to-Adapt Pathology, Features and Immediate Treatment
units.guide:
Symptomatic chronic AR goes directly to aortic valve replacement; asymptomatic severe AR uses the 55–50 rule, EF ≤55% or LVEDD ≥50% (p317).
Acute AR follows aortic dissection with chest pain, infective endocarditis, ruptured sinus of Valsalva with right-heart failure, or trauma. With no time to adapt, raised LVEDP and LAP >25 mmHg cause acute pulmonary edema and LV failure; the EDM is short and low pitched with soft S1 and LVF can produce cardiogenic shock and hypotension.
Immediate surgery is definitive. While awaiting surgery, NTG, nitroprusside and inotropes are grouped together as lowering aortic pressure.
